Sean Carroll – a theoretical physicist and outspoken scientific realist – has consistently argued against “consciousness-first” models of the cosmos. He maintains that physicalist explanations suffice, and that proposals like panpsychism or quantum idealism add unnecessary baggage. Below we break down Carroll’s major critiques, his epistemological approach (Bayesian reasoning and realism), and highlights from recent talks and debates where he clashes with mind-centric theories.

Panpsychism – “consciousness everywhere” – is a prime target of Carroll’s criticism. This view posits that all matter has some element of consciousness, so that assembling many “conscious” particles yields higher consciousness. Carroll finds this both unhelpful and implausible. He notes that panpsychism offers no testable predictions and no clear mechanism by which tiny proto-consciousness units combine into our complex awareness. In debates (e.g. with philosopher Philip Goff), Carroll emphasizes that materialism can in principle explain consciousness and does not obviously fail so badly that we must declare consciousness a new fundamental ingredient. He points out that simply asserting “consciousness all the way down” is vacuous – unless one specifies how it affects physical behavior, it has no explanatory power. As he succinctly put it, “I know that I [am] made of all these atoms and they’re all obeying the laws of physics. There’s no room in there for anything else.” In other words, nothing in known physics suggests we must imbue electrons or rocks with mental properties to get human consciousness. Carroll argues that adding mental properties to fundamental particles either: (a) does nothing (if those properties don’t affect particle behavior), or (b) contradicts known physics (if they do have physical effects). Neither option is appealing – the former makes the theory useless, and the latter demands rewriting well-tested physics. “Quantum idealism” or consciousness-based physics interpretations fare no better under Carroll’s scrutiny. He firmly rejects the notion that quantum mechanics requires a conscious observer to “collapse” the wavefunction. In fact, Carroll is a proponent of the Many-Worlds Interpretation, which treats the wavefunction as real and ever-branching, with no special role for measurement by a mind. He has lampooned the habit of linking quantum mysteries with consciousness as a mistake of conflating two unknowns – “Here’s something we don’t understand; here’s something else we don’t understand; hopefully there’s a connection between them.” . In his view, quantum mechanics works perfectly well with purely physical processes; for instance, interactions with the environment (decoherence) explain why specific outcomes appear, without

invoking any “mind force.” Carroll often stresses that the universe got along fine for billions of years before life evolved, so quantum events clearly don’t wait for human observers. He therefore labels consciousness-centric quantum theories as “nonsense” or mysticism, not serious science. For example, he dismisses philosopher Donald Hoffman’s radical idealism – the claim that space, time, and physics are mere artifacts of observation – as deeply misguided. When asked to consider Hoffman’s idea that the physical world is just a user interface hiding an underlying reality of minds, Carroll responded that part of that perspective (“we might not know the ultimate ontology”) is reasonable, but the leap to “spacetime is an illusion” is “just wrong.” Our current framework may be incomplete, but it captures real, structural truths about the world. Declaring the known world an illusion, he argues, confuses an evolving scientific model with a fantasy. In short, Carroll finds no merit in interpretations that put consciousness before physics – physical law comes first, mind emerges later. As he told Lex Fridman, even the subjective feeling of “redness” or pain is “a certain way of talking about the atoms and neurons” in our brain – a high-level description of physical processes, just as “temperature” is a description of molecular motion. He sees no mystery that forces us to treat mind as separate from matter: “I see no reason to change the laws of physics to account for [consciousness].” In contrast to these mind-first views, Carroll champions a sober physicalism. He acknowledges that we don’t yet fully understand how consciousness arises from the brain’s circuitry – it’s a hard problem – but he’s confident this is a question of emergent complexity, not of new fundamental substances. In Carroll’s metaphor, consciousness is like software running on the “hardware” of neurons, not an extra ghostly ingredient. It is an emergent property of matter arranged in exceedingly intricate ways. Just as wetness “emerges” from H₂O molecules (and we don’t need a vital liquid essence to explain it), consciousness can emerge from physical interactions in the brain without assuming that electrons have minds. Carroll even suggests the so-called “Hard Problem” of consciousness may gradually evaporate – as neuroscience advances, we’ll dissolve the intuitive mystery and see consciousness as a natural result of certain organizational patterns. In one public dialogue, he predicted that

as we learn more, the question “what is it like to be me?” will stop seeming magical – we will understand it in terms of information processing, just as we came to understand life or planetary motion in physical terms. This stance sharply contrasts with panpsychists who consider the hard problem a permanent roadblock requiring a paradigm shift. Carroll’s retort is that declaring consciousness fundamental is an act of desperation, not a solution – it papers over ignorance with an unfalsifiable claim. Instead, he trusts that ordinary physics, applied to extraordinarily complex systems, is enough to eventually explain our mental experience. In summary, he deems panpsychism and related ideas unnecessary, untestable, and unjustified, preferring to stick with the working recipe of science: matter and energy arranged by physical laws, producing higher-level phenomena like mind when conditions are right.

Underpinning Carroll’s critique is his philosophy-of-science outlook. He is a staunch scientific realist – meaning he believes our best theories aim to describe reality as it is, not just save appearances. For Carroll, the entities and laws postulated by physics (fields, particles, the quantum wavefunction, etc.) are real aspects of the world . This outlook demands that any new theory, even a speculative one about consciousness, must earn its credence by fitting into the established empirical framework or by predicting new observable facts. Carroll often invokes the idea of the “Core Theory” – essentially the Standard Model of particle physics plus general relativity, which together account for all known non-gravitational phenomena at everyday scales. This core theory has been enormously successful and tested to high precision. Thus, he argues, the burden of proof is on any rival or extension that claims, for example, that in addition to electrons having mass, charge, spin, “each electron has a tiny consciousness.” It’s not that such a thing is flat-out impossible, but if it were true, it should have left some imprint in our experiments. Carroll illustrates this with a concrete example: if electrons possessed new mental degrees of freedom (say “happy” or “sad” states in addition to

spin up/down), quantum field theory would allow those states to contribute to particle interactions. We would see signs of additional quantum states in particle scattering data – which we decidedly do not. As he quips, “we know empirically how many degrees of freedom actual electrons have” (two spin states for an electron, and two for its antiparticle) – any hidden mental states would “have an unmistakable impact” on outcomes, “in flagrant contradiction with experiment.” . This kind of hard-nosed argument exemplifies Carroll’s insistence that new theories meet the same empirical standards as established physics. It’s not enough to say “imagine all particles have consciousness” – one must say how that interacts (or doesn’t) with their charges and motions. As he writes, any viable proposal “must specify one of two alternatives: [either] changing the known laws of physics, or positing that [the mental aspects] exert no causal influence over physical behavior.” If you change the laws, you’d better do so with the rigor of a physicist – spell out the new dynamics and show they haven’t already been ruled out. If you go the other route (mind has zero influence on matter), then the “consciousness” you added is literally undetectable in principle – a metaphysical ghost that might as well not exist. Carroll finds the latter “even less promising” because it makes consciousness irrelevant to everything that happens in the universe. After all, our only handle on consciousness is via behavior (including verbal reports, brain signals, etc.), so a property that can never affect behavior is useless in explaining why we talk about consciousness at all. Carroll approaches these matters in a Bayesian, evidence-weighting manner. Instead of treating a speculative idea as just philosophically intriguing, he asks: How well does it score on simplicity and empirical support? Panpsychism or “mind-first” cosmologies start with a very low prior probability in his assessment – because they complicate our ontology (adding an entire mental aspect to every particle) without any prior successes to justify that move. Meanwhile, the null hypothesis (consciousness emerges from complex neurons following known physics) has a lot going for it: it meshes with the rest of science and with abundant evidence linking mind to brain. Thus, one would need extraordinarily strong new evidence to overcome the prior and favor a consciousness-centric physics. So far, no such evidence

exists. Carroll often emphasizes that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; by default, you don’t abandon a successful paradigm for a radical new one just because a problem is hard. He also cautions against unfalsifiable “ad hoc stories.” In an essay on scientific method, he noted that from a Bayesian perspective, theories that simply accommodate any outcome with a flexible story are penalized – they don’t get a pass just because they can wiggle around counter-evidence. This attitude applies to many consciousness-centric ideas, which can be maddeningly vague. (For example, if someone says “consciousness is everywhere” yet it magically never alters any particle’s behavior in measurable ways, that theory can “explain” anything and thus, in Bayesian terms, explains nothing.) Carroll has explicitly argued against loosening our scientific standards for such ideas. He disagrees with the claim that consciousness is beyond science or that we need new metaphysical principles to tackle it. Instead, he trusts in “continuing the ordinary program of understanding the brain” – using neuroscience and cognitive science within the current physicalist framework. The confirmation of theories, for Carroll, comes when they make successful predictions or unify phenomena in a precise way. By that measure, panpsychism and quantum-consciousness notions haven’t earned any credence. They are “possibilities” in the abstract, but have not yet passed a single experimental or observational test. In fact, Carroll points out that our confidence in known physics (within its domain) is extremely high, whereas our grasp on consciousness is admittedly “fuzzy” – but that very contrast is why we should expect the solution to consciousness to come from extending our understanding of brain physics, not by overthrowing the basic physics itself. As he concludes in one paper, “The most promising route to understanding consciousness is likely to involve further neuroscientific insights and a more refined philosophical understanding of weak emergence, rather than rethinking the fundamental nature of reality.” In other words, betting on neurons and emergent complexity is a far better strategy than betting on a wholesale revision of what we consider real. This scientific-realist, Bayesian mindset explains why Carroll remains deeply skeptical of
Hoffman’s universe of “conscious agents” or Wolfram’s hypergraph physics or any other maverick theory until and unless they demonstrate tangible explanatory gains.

Thomas Aquinas explicitly discusses God’s knowledge as the cause of things (rather than a mere reflection of them) in Quaestiones Disputatae de Veritate (“Disputed Questions on Truth”), Question 2 (on God’s Knowledge), Article 14. This article directly asks, “Is God’s knowledge the cause of things?” . Aquinas answers yes, drawing a sharp contrast between divine knowledge and human knowledge. In this context, he emphasizes that whereas human knowers discover truth by conforming to reality, God’s knowledge establishes reality – creation conforms to the divine mind. Below are key

quotations from De Veritate q.2 a.14 that illustrate this point, especially Aquinas’s use of the artisan analogy and the idea that things are true because God made them according to His knowledge . ● “Not because they are does God know all creatures, spiritual and corporeal, but they are because He knows them.” Aquinas here quotes St. Augustine, affirming that God’s knowledge is logically prior to created things. In other words, creatures exist in the way that they do because God knows (and wills) them so – not the other way around. This reverses the order we experience as humans. For us, a thing must exist or be true for our minds to know it. But in God’s case, His knowing a thing is what causes it to be. Aquinas immediately draws the conclusion: “Therefore, God’s knowledge is the cause of created things.” ● “God’s knowledge is, in a sense, the art of the things that are to be created; hence Augustine says: ‘The Word is an artistic conception filled with the intelligible characters of living things.’ But art is the cause of artistic products. Therefore, God’s knowledge is the cause of created things.” . Here Aquinas invokes an analogy of God as an artisan. The Divine Word (Logos) – which is God’s perfect idea of Himself and all that could be – is likened to an artist’s conception or blueprint containing the “intelligible characters” (inner designs) of all creatures. Just as an artisan’s art (skill and design in his mind) is the cause of the artifact he produces, God’s knowledge serves as the exemplar model that things follow. In scholastic terms, God’s knowledge is like an exemplar cause – the divine intellect is the master plan according to which all creatures are made. Creation is thus analogous to an artifact that has been crafted to match the idea in the craftsman’s mind. Aquinas uses this analogy to show that divine knowledge does not passively mirror things; rather, created things actively mirror the divine ideas. They are true and orderly because they express God’s “art”. ● “Hence, there is left only one possibility: His knowledge is the cause of things. Conversely, our knowledge is caused by things inasmuch as we receive it from things.” . In Aquinas’s own reply, he sets out the metaphysical either-or: in any knowing relationship, either the knower’s knowledge causes the thing or vice versa. For God, the latter is impossible (a temporal thing cannot cause God’s eternal knowledge). Thus, Aquinas concludes that God’s knowledge alone must be the cause of things. He explicitly contrasts this with human knowledge, which is effect , not cause: we come to know things by receiving impressions of reality. God, however, knows things by producing them. In short, “the way things are” corresponds to God’s knowledge because He made them to fit the ideas in His intellect. The world’s order and truth reflect the fact that “the things known by God proceed from His knowledge” (whereas our knowledge proceeds from the things).

Aquinas develops this teaching in a rich theological and philosophical context. De Veritate Q.2 as a whole deals with the nature of divine knowledge. Article 14 comes after Aquinas has already shown that God knows all things, including singulars and future contingents, in one simple eternal act. The specific concern in Article 14 is whether God’s knowledge is merely speculative (like ours, which depends on things as its object) or practical/exemplary, actually giving rise to things. Aquinas frames the debate by citing Origen’s opinion that “a thing will be, not because God knows... but, because it will be, it is known by God before it exists”. In other words, Origen held that God’s foreknowledge follows the creature’s actual existence (to preserve creaturely freedom). Aquinas rejects this order. Aligning with St. Augustine and the tradition of divine ideas, he argues that God’s knowledge precedes and underlies created reality . Augustine taught that the exemplar of every creature resides in the Divine Word, and Aquinas echoes this: “the Word is an artistic conception” containing the forms of creatures. Thus, God’s knowing is a creative, artisan-like knowledge. This is a theological affirmation of God’s sovereignty and providence: all things depend on the divine intellect and will. Metaphysically, it reflects the principle that being and truth in creatures are a participation in the perfect being and truth of God. A created thing is true insofar as it fulfills the idea in the divine mind . As Aquinas explains earlier, “things... cannot exist except by reason of the divine intellect which keeps bringing them into being… a thing is said to be true principally because of its order to the truth of the divine intellect” . He explains that God’s knowledge causes things through the medium of His will (and through secondary causes in the created order). This preserves the metaphysical distinction that God is the first cause (with knowledge and will united in Him), while creatures exercise their own causal powers under God’s ordinance. This insight situates truth and knowledge firmly in a theological-metaphysical framework: all truth in things flows from the eternal Truth of God, who made all things according to His wise knowledge. Gathering this dataset required a systematic literature search across multiple databases (e.g., Google Scholar, CrossRef, Web of Science) and reference lists. We then searched for academic publications from 2014–2024 that cite these works or otherwise reference the individual by name in a citation context (including in-text citations, footnotes, endnotes, or reference lists). Inclusion criteria: We included peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, academic book chapters, dissertations, and preprints, as long as they were in English and had an identifiable citation to one of the nine individuals’ work. Each citing publication is treated as a single entry in the dataset. If a paper cited works by multiple of the listed thinkers, it is tagged under all relevant names (for example, a neuroscience paper might reference both Friston’s and Levin’s work). We also noted the citation type – for instance, citations in science and social science papers typically appear in a reference list, whereas in humanities (like theology) they may appear in footnotes or endnotes. The project developed in this dialogue begins from a recognition of profound fracture: in philosophy, in the sciences, and in the communities that sustain human inquiry. The physicalist orthodoxy that continues to dominate contemporary academic life—most coherently articulated in Sean Carroll’s The Big Picture —insists that the universe is fundamentally composed of mindless matter obeying impersonal laws. On such a view, consciousness, intelligence, and life emerge late, as complex but ultimately reducible phenomena, incidental byproducts of the combinatorial evolution of simpler physical structures. In sharp contrast, the project proposed here advances a hypothesis of conscious realism: that conscious agents and their interactions constitute the fundamental substrate of reality. On this view, what we call space, time, causality, and materiality emerge from structured networks of conscious activity. Being, Life, and Intelligence are not belated appearances in a mechanical universe; they are primary realities, the generative patterns from which all stable structures—including those described by physics—arise. This alone, however, does not fully describe the ambition of the project. A crucial distinction must be made between two intertwined aims: First, the formation of an interdisciplinary research community—a team—organized around the emerging paradigm of Christic Morphogenic Conscious Realism.

Second, the articulation of a meta-disciplinary operating system—the game rules—for structuring rational, tradition-aware, dialectical engagement among rival paradigms and research communities. The first aim addresses the immediate need: the world is not now populated by richly-developed, internally coherent traditions of inquiry prepared to undertake dialogue about first principles. Modernity has fragmented once-coherent intellectual and communal inheritances, leaving individuals and disciplines atomized. Thus, the initial task is bootstrap: to enrich partial communities, to form a coherent, cross-disciplinary team around promising attractors—in this case, the attractors organized by Christic Morphogenic Conscious Realism. The second aim, however, points beyond any particular team or tradition. Even a flourishing paradigm—no matter how compelling internally—cannot validate itself without structured confrontation with rival perspectives. The ultimate measure of a paradigm’s power lies not in its internal coherence alone, but in its capacity to survive, integrate, and enrich itself through engagement with other mature traditions. Therefore, the deeper task is to design and pilot the game rules: the conditions and procedures by which communities enter into rational, critical, and transformative dialogue with one another. This is the task of the master science: the science of rational communal self-transcendence through structured dialectic. Importantly, Christic Morphogenic Conscious Realism is not proposed as the master science itself. It is a candidate team paradigm: a research tradition in formation that must enter the arena of rational contestation structured by the master science. Its success or failure, ultimately, depends not solely upon its internal achievements but upon its performance in open, rule-governed engagement with rivals. The dual structure of the project thus becomes clear:

Biologist and computer scientist Michael Levin is among the researchers who have discovered how to effect inheritance via nongenetic, non-epigenetic bioelectric programming stored in ion channels. Such programming stores goals, not recipes for achieving them. Morphogenic studies (on the development of shape) have shown that biological entities from the simplest cells to complex organisms act not as mechanistic units but as distributed problem-solvers. Bioelectric circuits among cells store pattern memories, model (sometimes multiple) target morphologies, and guide repairs when deviations occur. Much of this behavior is extraordinary: planarian worms reproduce with inheritable 2nd heads without DNA-level changes. Damaged Xenobots reconfigure themselves to achieve locomotion using tools evolution never trained them to use. Such behavior suggests goal-directed modeling at the cellular level. In addition to guiding the shape of cells and organisms, bioelectric memory guides the development of identity: each biological unit’s sense of self vs its external environment. Levin’s ambitious and already-productive research plan is to learn to map bioelectric memory through to morphology and identity, supporting intervention in either to repair or build new kinds of life. Psychiatrist and brain mapper Karl Friston is perhaps the most cited neuroscientist in the world. His Free Energy Principle reframes cognition and life as the continual minimization of surprise. Every system that persists over time, from a single cell to a brain, predicts its environment and acts to reduce errors in that prediction. His formulation of active inference offers a mathematical account of agency, and his published collaborations with Levin extend this logic to developmental biology. Technologist, Palm-Pilot inventor and theoretical neuroscientist Jeff Hawkins describes the human neocortex as a hive-mind. In it, 100,000 differently-wired neocortical columns—about 100, or 1% of them, are active at any one time, processing the same sensory input. This amounts to a parallel-processing motherboard, on which each cortical column creates its own full-world model based on complementary versions of sensorimotor experience. Consensus emerges through electrochemical voting. Here we see a plurality of organisms (the neocortical columns) subordinated to a larger self—us—precisely as Levin describes at the cellular level, operating at the highest levels of biological intelligence known to us. Hawkins steers clear of discussions of consciousness; he himself is not a conscious realist proponent. But the detailed picture he provides of the inner workings of the human brain tracks tightly with the interactive agency of the conscious realist model. Moreover, his work provides a clear case of separate cognitive entities being combined into a single self that is conscious of itself only as a single self, and not of any intelligence of what have become its parts. This is an explicit, plausible case of multiple cognitive agents functioning as parts of a single conscious whole, the core assertion of conscious realism. Iain McGilchrist, a psychiatrist and literary scholar, offers a phenomenological and neurobiological account of how the two brain hemispheres model the world differently.

The right hemisphere perceives context and relation, while the left abstracts and manipulates. Conscious Realism echoes this asymmetry, favoring relational modeling as ontologically prior. More importantly, the two-hemisphere system of which McGilchrist is the world’s leading scholar itself illustrates the subordination of (in this case) two conscious elements, neither of which knows of the other but who work together to form a whole self, itself conscious of neither component, but only of itself, the whole. Astonishingly, when the bridge between those two components is severed (in an operation called a corpus callostomy), both components (left and right brains) function independently, each conscious of itself, not the other, and not the whole. To conscious realists, this system is proof of concept that separate cognitive agents unite to form wholes. This fusion of cognitive elements into a single consciousness follows from the mathematics of consciousness developed by Donald Hoffman, Professor of Cognitive and Computer Sciences and Philosophy at UC Irvine, and his colleague, mathematician Chetan Prekash. In their view, the physical world is an interface evolved for fitness, not truth. What we see is not reality but a user interface—structured output from deeper conscious dynamics. Hoffman has been the foremost and longest public advocate of conscious realism. Particularly attractive is his attempt to bridge the mathematics of consciousness with a new mathematical foundation for replacing space-time with complex hypergraphs such as the amplituhedron, a project of Physicist Nema Arkani-Hamed and colleagues, from which the laws of physics may emerge. This is clear research path toward solving the hard problem of the physical world: how it emerges from the interactions of conscious agents. That prominence has made Hoffman attractive on the podcast circuit, where he appears often either asynchronously or together with Stephen Wolfram, author of Mathematica and a host of other computations products. Future Research Agenda If Conscious Realism is to move from an emerging paradigm to a mature tradition of inquiry, it must be fertile. That means it must not only explain what has already been discovered, but generate new questions, predictions, and programs of investigation. What follows is not a speculative roadmap, but a sketch of some immediate next steps visible from the convergence already underway. These are offered as representative attractors to the CR paradigm, a measure of its likelihood to succeed in dialectical engagement with other traditions in the quest for dollars and talent. First, there is the need to formalize further the mathematics of agent interaction. Hoffman’s model of conscious agents offers one approach; Wolfram’s graph-theoretic framework offers another. Both derive physical laws from interaction-based formalisms.

These approaches need to be extended and compared: how does the observer-relativity in Wolfram’s hypergraphs correspond to the compositional updating of Hoffman’s agents? Can they be mapped or unified in a shared mathematical framework? Second, Levin’s attempt to map bioelectric memory through to morphology and cellular identity is in its infancy, and will require a broadly interdisciplinary and well-funded effort. That map has essential implications regarding birth defect prevention and treatment, injury repair, and aging. But here we should pause to note just its implications for cancer research. Cancer, on Levin’s model, is what cells ordinarily do when they are acting as isolated selves in a body that amounts to its external world: eat, multiply, and colonize. Levin’s team has already succeed in treating cancer by telling a class of carcinogenic cells that they belong to the whole body, accomplished through chemical intervention in ion channels to relink cells bioelectrically with their neighbors. This is perhaps as strong an attractor as is currently being explored under this paradigm. But perhaps there is a still stronger attractor in the same neighborhood. Those militant cancer cells, cut off from their identity with the whole body and caring only for themselves, are reminiscent of human international relations. Does Fredrickson’s model of emotional synchrony belong in a new tab in Levin’s map? Current work is siloed by institutional and disciplinary norms. Conscious Realism offers a conceptual attractor already shown capable of drawing together neuroscience, physics, information theory, developmental biology, and systems psychology, and it seems to make promise for still other sciences, including sociology. Creating shared platforms, common formal tools, and collaborative protocols will be essential to test the full force of the paradigm. Testing the attractors inherent in the conscious realist paradigm and those of its rivals is just what is required to show that CR is not just useful, but true.
